clue.text: Arduous improvised solo in musical accompaniment

indicators.note: the solo is placed in the accompaniment, so one word sits inside the other

parts.note: backing is the accompaniment behind a singer or soloist
a break in jazz is a short improvised solo passage

explanation.surface: A demanding ad-libbed solo played over the band's accompaniment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts BREAK inside BACKING, splitting it after BACK.
explanation.definitionFit: Work that strains your back is exhausting and laborious, hence the sense of very hard going.

clue.text: Bird is unpalatable? Not to start with

parts.note: a bitter taste is unpleasant, so unpalatable

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word is wanted

explanation.surface: A diner asks whether a bird tastes bad and is told not at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to start with' takes the first letter of 'Not', added after BITTER.
explanation.definitionFit: The bittern is a heron-like marsh bird known for its booming call.

clue.text: About to show a leg and get up

parts.note: C stands for circa, Latin for about with dates
a leg is a limb

explanation.surface: Someone is on the point of revealing a leg and rising.
explanation.definitionFit: To climb is to ascend or go up, as up a ladder or hill.

clue.text: General direction of attack

parts.note: broad means general, as in broad terms
a side is a direction or quarter, as in from every side

explanation.surface: An army commander's line of assault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General' looks like a military officer but is an adjective meaning broad.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadside is the firing of all guns on one side of a warship, and figuratively a fierce verbal onslaught.

clue.text: Be up to no good

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: to be is to live or exist

explanation.surface: Getting up to mischief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' in this down clue reverses LIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something evil is wicked, the opposite of good.

clue.text: Punish sailor in ship on tow

indicators.note: in a down entry, one part placed on another stands above it

parts.note: keel is a poetic word for a ship
to haul is to tow or drag

explanation.surface: A seaman is disciplined aboard by being dragged behind the vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' in a down clue places KEEL above HAUL. Keelhauling dragged an offender under a ship's keel.
explanation.definitionFit: Keelhauling was a naval punishment of dragging a seaman under the hull from one side to the other.

clue.text: In the war, Granny longed for some of this

definitions.text: In the war, Granny longed for some of this

indicators.note: only part of these words is used, the run of letters sitting across them

explanation.surface: A grandmother recalls craving stockings during wartime shortages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some of' takes the run across 'graNNY LONged'. Nylon stockings were scarce in Britain in the Second World War, so the whole clue is also the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Nylon, the synthetic fibre used for stockings, was a coveted luxury in wartime rationing.

clue.text: Game said to feature many clubs

explanation.surface: A sport supposedly involving lots of clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: Pall-mall was an old mallet-and-ball game; Pall Mall is a London street famous for its gentlemen's clubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Pall-mall was a game played with mallets, and the London street named after it is lined with private members' clubs.

clue.text: Stiffness of celebrity with companion

parts.note: a star is a celebrity
CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A famous person brings a stiff, formal companion.
explanation.walkthrough: CH is Companion of Honour, an award in the British honours system.
explanation.definitionFit: Starch is used to stiffen fabric, so it also means formality or rigidity.

clue.text: Bitter 'oil could be extracted from this old sea-creature

indicators.note: the letters of the two words can be drawn out and rearranged to give something new

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bitter oil might be squeezed out of some ancient marine animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be extracted from' signals rearranging the nine letters of BITTER OIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Trilobites were marine arthropods that died out hundreds of millions of years ago, known now only as fossils.

clue.text: Smallest schoolboy is at end of line

indicators.note: the schoolboy comes after the line, placed at its end

parts.note: East is Tom Brown's friend in the Victorian school novel Tom Brown's Schooldays

explanation.surface: The littlest pupil has to stand at the back of the queue.
explanation.walkthrough: The schoolboy is East, Tom Brown's chum in Thomas Hughes's Tom Brown's Schooldays, a classic novel of an English boarding school; 'at end of' puts him after L.
explanation.definitionFit: Least is the superlative of little, meaning the tiniest of all.

clue.text: The downfall of Dombey, to give an example

indicators.note: the name collapses and its letters fall into a new order

explanation.surface: The ruin of Dickens's Mr Dombey serves as an illustration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The downfall of' rearranges DOMBEY, the merchant of Dickens's Dombey and Son.
explanation.definitionFit: To embody something is to be a concrete instance or personification of it.

clue.text: Dealer in thrillers?

parts.note: a shopkeeper selling supplies, and also the American writer of hard-boiled detective novels such as The Big Sleep

explanation.surface: Someone who trades in exciting crime novels.
explanation.walkthrough: A ship's chandler is a dealer in supplies; Raymond Chandler wrote thrillers, so he 'deals in' them in another sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A chandler is a dealer in provisions or candles, and Raymond Chandler was a famous author of crime thrillers.

clue.text: Be inattentive and spill ink — get a cloth

parts.note: to nap is to be off guard or not paying attention, as in caught napping

indicators.note: spilt ink is scattered, so its letters land in a new order

explanation.surface: A careless writer knocks over the inkpot and reaches for something to mop it up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spill' rearranges INK into KIN, which follows NAP.
explanation.definitionFit: A napkin is a small square of cloth used at table for wiping the mouth and hands.

clue.text: Leave vehicle and alight in grassy area.

parts.note: to park is to leave a car standing
to land is to alight, come down from flight

explanation.surface: Stop the car and get out on to some open lawns.
explanation.definitionFit: Parkland is open grassland with scattered trees, as around a country house.

clue.text: Almost have to stamp on rat

indicators.note: the word is not quite complete, losing its last letter

parts.note: must means have to, as in you must go
to quash a rebellion is to stamp on it, suppressing it

explanation.surface: An urge to tread on a rodent, nearly irresistible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' drops the last letter of MUST to leave MUS. The rat is the muskrat, whose old name is musquash.
explanation.definitionFit: Musquash is another name for the muskrat, a large North American water rodent.

clue.text: Greatly increase times for speaking

explanation.surface: Times for speaking get much longer.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense works when spoken: 'times for' sounds like 'times four', which is what multiplying fourfold is.
explanation.definitionFit: To quadruple is to multiply by four, a big increase, and spoken as times four.

clue.text: Priest nearly goes on to fashion a rhyme

indicators.note: the word falls just short, missing its last letter

parts.note: a cleric is a priest or clergyman
to hew is to shape or fashion by cutting

explanation.surface: A clergyman almost goes on to shape a verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly' drops the final C of CLERIC. A clerihew is a comic four-line verse about a famous person.
explanation.definitionFit: A clerihew is a short humorous biographical verse of four lines, named after E. Clerihew Bentley.

clue.text: King Charles to look from the tower

parts.note: Charles Martel was the eighth-century Frankish ruler, here loosely called king
lo is an old exclamation meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: A monarch gazes out from a high turret.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Martel, 'the Hammer', ruled the Franks; LO is the archaic call to look. A Martello tower is a small round coastal fort built in Britain against Napoleon.
explanation.definitionFit: Martello towers are squat circular forts built along British coasts in the Napoleonic era.

clue.text: Girl is my wife

parts.note: miss is a girl or young unmarried woman

explanation.surface: A girl turns out to be the speaker's spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: The missis is an informal term a husband uses for his wife.

clue.text: Say we're thick-skinned, with this

parts.note: split into two words, the answer is what you would say to label us as tough, and it is also a patch of hardened skin

explanation.surface: Someone insists that they and others are insensitive.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as CALL US it means 'say we're'; whole, it is a thickened patch of skin, so having one leaves you literally thick-skinned.
explanation.definitionFit: A callus is a toughened, hardened area of skin built up by repeated friction.

clue.text: City letters held up by poor spelling

indicators.note: the letters are held within the other word, enclosed by it

parts.note: sorry means poor or wretched, as in a sorry state

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: EC is the London postcode for the City, its financial district

explanation.surface: Bad spelling holds up a city's correspondence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns EC (the City of London postcode) into CE, which 'held' puts inside SORRY.
explanation.definitionFit: A spell is a magic charm, so spelling is witchcraft or sorcery.

clue.text: Sort of imprisonment of soul, .-. it's said

explanation.surface: Some kind of punishment that locks up the spirit, people say.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a pun: spoken, the word sounds like an adjective made from 'soul', soul-itary, as sanitary is from sanity.
explanation.definitionFit: Solitary is short for solitary confinement in jail, and punningly sounds like a word meaning relating to the spirit.

clue.text: Announced imposition keeps changing

indicators.note: spoken out, the word for a levy sounds like the answer

parts.note: a tax is an imposition or levy

explanation.surface: A newly declared levy is constantly altered.
explanation.walkthrough: A sailing boat tacks when it changes course, so a boat that tacks keeps changing direction.
explanation.definitionFit: To tack is to change course while sailing against the wind, so it means repeatedly changing.

clue.text: Find the right sort of bullet

parts.note: to trace a missing person is to find them

explanation.surface: Choose the correct type of ammunition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tracer round contains a burning compound that leaves a visible trail to show its flight path.

clue.text: Fawn brought up with colt originally — would you believe it

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word is taken
in a down entry, bringing a word up reverses it

parts.note: a fawn is a young deer

explanation.surface: A young deer was reared with a colt, amazingly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'originally' gives C from colt; 'brought up' reverses DEER to REED.
explanation.definitionFit: A creed is a set of beliefs, what you would hold as true.

clue.text: Overdone in Shakespeare, the wife in 'evil surroundings

indicators.note: the word for evil forms surroundings for the wife

parts.note: bad means evil or wicked

explanation.surface: Too much Shakespeare surrounds a wife with wickedness.
explanation.walkthrough: Mistress Overdone is the brothel-keeper in Shakespeare's Measure for Measure, so 'Overdone' is a name, not 'excessive'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mistress Overdone is a madam, and a bawd is a woman who keeps a brothel.

clue.text: Sort of order superhuman executed

indicators.note: an executed person may be beheaded, so the word loses its first letter

parts.note: bionic, from the TV Bionic Man, means having superhuman powers

explanation.surface: A kind of command carried out by some superhuman being.
explanation.walkthrough: 'executed' means beheaded: BIONIC loses its B. 'order' is architectural, not a command.
explanation.definitionFit: Ionic is one of the classical orders of architecture, with scroll-shaped capitals on its columns.

clue.text: Man of intellect found to lead chapter

explanation.surface: A clever person turns out to head a section of the book.
explanation.walkthrough: A headpiece is an old word for the head or intellect and, by extension, a clever person; in printing it is the ornament at the head of a chapter.
explanation.definitionFit: Headpiece means a brain or brainy person, and also a decorative printed design placed at the top of a chapter.

clue.text: Eliot wrote it fast

explanation.surface: The poet wrote something quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fast' is not speed but a day of fasting, the first day of Lent; T. S. Eliot's 1930 poem has the same title.
explanation.definitionFit: T. S. Eliot's poem takes its title from the Christian day of fasting and penance that begins Lent.
